Can the Sphere Encoder make a video?

5-second clips from an open video model (Wan2.1, 16 fps, 81 frames each). For every clip we ask two things of a frozen Sphere Encoder 2: can it hold every frame, starting from the first, and can it predict the next frame on its own? Sections 1 to 4 train nothing; sections 5 and 6 train small predictors on top of the frozen encoder and decoder.

The rotation idea on the sphere: how far vs which way

The rotation model (section 6) splits each prediction in two: how far frame t is from frame 0 (an angle) and which way it went (a direction at frame 0). The prediction is frame 0 turned by that angle in that direction, so on this view it sits on a straight spoke out of the north pole. Like giving directions from a city: "20 miles" plus "north-east". Dark = the real video, purple = the rotation model, green dashed = the model's distance with the true direction (a cheat that shows what a correct direction would buy). At the playing frame, the two spokes from the pole show the direction gap as a wedge, and the dashed rings show the two distances. The wedge label is the real direction gap; the picture squeezes hundreds of directions into two, so the wedge can look narrower than its label.

2. Predicting the next frame

Given the two previous true latents, predict the next one. Error is the angle on the sphere to the true next latent (lower is better). A path with momentum would let "keep going" beat "copy".

3. Rolling out 5 seconds from two frames

Start from the first two true frames and predict every later frame from the model's own previous outputs. LPIPS against the true frame, averaged per second (lower is better; 0.07 is what the search reaches).

5. Learning the motion: a frame predictor

A small network g(z₀, t) takes the first frame's latent and a frame number and outputs that frame's latent (a step away from z₀ on the sphere). Encoder and decoder stay frozen. Trained on all the training clips above, then tested on new clips from new prompts it never saw. The bar to beat is "freeze the first frame".

6. Splitting the rotation: how far vs which way

Getting from frame 0 to frame X on the sphere is one rotation, and a rotation has two parts: how far to turn (one number, an angle) and which way to turn (a direction among about 98,000). Think of a pilot leaving an airport: distance and heading. This model has a separate output for each, trained against the true angle and the true direction, so we can score each half on its own. Same 24 training clips, same 16 new test clips, frames 2 to 80.

7. What each model generated, side by side

Every model gets only the first frame of a new test clip (plus frame 1 for the hinted rotation model) and generates frames 2 to 80. Same 5 seconds, all tiles in sync. The last tile is a cheat that uses the true direction, to show how much the "how far" part alone is worth. A grey tile means that model was not scored on this clip.

What this means

  • Holding works. A latent that draws each frame exists right next to the previous frame's latent, and quality does not decay over 5 seconds.
  • Predicting does not. The latent path turns almost at random from one frame to the next, so geometric extrapolation and a linear fitted map both lose to copying the last frame, and rollouts break down within about a second.
  • A small trained predictor memorises instead of generalising. Trained on the training clips it replays them well from their first frame, but on new prompts it is worse than freezing the first frame on every test clip (Section 5): with this few videos it learns those videos, not motion.
  • Splitting the rotation shows exactly where it fails (Section 6). "How far" is easy: the model is about 4° off, no better than a plain average curve. "Which way" is the whole problem: on new clips the predicted direction is about 81° off, close to a blind guess (90°), even when the model also sees the first two frames. Given the true direction, the model's distance alone beats freezing on 14 of 16 new clips (LPIPS 0.22, about the encoder re-draw level).
  • So generation needs learned motion, and far more data. A model of how the latent moves would have to be trained; the searched paths ( frame-to-frame steps here) are the data such a model would need. Vinayak found the same for camera moves: no useful linear rule.

Limits

  • clips, one seed each, generated (not real) video. Real-video comparison is the next step.
  • The search uses the true frames, so it is an upper bound, not generation. The best step is chosen by the same LPIPS the loss uses, so its score is slightly optimistic.
  • Search drift. The chained search drifts on its own: a frozen single-frame "video" still travels about 28° in 5 s (Section 4). Most of the searched path's long-range shape, and its distance from the encoder's latents, is this drift, not motion. A fix is to anchor each search to the encoder latent of its own frame.
